transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you so much for fitting me in. I, um... well, it feels a little silly to even say out loud, so I really hope you don't think I'm just being vain. But I guess I'm here because I've been having a really hard time with... with my face. 

I just can't stop seeing this awful droop and unevenness around my mouth and my jaw. It's in every single photo, every reflection, and it's just... it's all I can focus on. People tell me I look fine, and I try to believe them, I really do, but to me, it's just so glaringly obvious. 

It's actually gotten to the point where I'm, um... I've started avoiding my presentations at work, and I'm finding excuses not to meet with clients. Which is terrible for an architect, I know. I feel awful about it. Does... does that make sense? I hope I'm explaining this right.
Do you think other people can see this droop and unevenness in your face when they look at you?

I know I just mentioned that people tell me I look fine... and I really don't want to sound ungrateful, because I know they're just trying to be nice. But, um... yes. Deep down, I feel like they absolutely must see it. 

I mean, it's just so prominent to me. Like I was saying, the droop and the unevenness around my jaw... it's there in every single reflection. So when I'm supposed to be leading a presentation or sitting across from a new client, I just freeze up. I feel like they're staring right at my mouth and just being too polite to say anything about how bad it looks. That's why I've been avoiding those meetings so much, even though I know I shouldn't. 

I'm sorry to repeat myself, I just... I hope that doesn't make me sound completely irrational. Am I explaining that okay?
Do you think it's possible that the droop and unevenness in your face are not as noticeable to others as they are to you?

I... well, I suppose it's possible. I really try to tell myself that, you know? That maybe it's just me being overly critical. I don't want to seem like I'm obsessed with my looks or anything. It's just... it's so hard when I look in the mirror or see a photo, and that unevenness around my mouth and jaw is the very first thing I see. It just feels so glaring to me. 

But you're right, maybe they don't notice it as much as I think they do. I just... I get so overwhelmed by the thought of them seeing it that I end up backing out of those client meetings and presentations anyway. I know it's silly, and I'm really trying to be better about it. Does that make sense? I hope I'm not being too difficult.
Do you think there's any possibility that the droop and unevenness you see in your face aren't actually there?

I... gosh, I really want to say yes, just because I know how crazy this all sounds. I want to agree with you, I really do, because I want to be a good patient. But... I just can't. I'm so sorry, I hope that doesn't frustrate you. 

It's just... that's exactly why I'm here. Because no matter how much I try to tell myself it's not real, or try to listen when people tell me I look fine, I just can't stop seeing it. The droop and the unevenness around my jaw... it's right there, staring back at me in every single photo and every reflection. It feels so undeniably, physically obvious to me. 

And it's just taken over, to the point where, like I mentioned, I'm hiding from my own clients and backing out of my presentations. I wish I could just snap out of it and say it's all in my head, I really do. Am I making any sense at all? I just want to be completely honest with you, even if it makes me sound a bit foolish.
Do you think that if a doctor or a plastic surgeon examined your face, they would find the droop and unevenness you see?

I... well, I haven't actually been to see a plastic surgeon or anything like that. I wouldn't want to waste their time, you know? And I really don't want to seem like someone who's just vain and chasing after perfection. 

But... if they did look, really closely? I don't know. Maybe they would say it's just normal aging, or that I'm blowing it out of proportion. I'm sure they see people with much worse problems all day long. So maybe they wouldn't see it as the glaring defect that I do. 

I'm sorry, I know I'm probably not giving you a very straight answer. I just... I guess I'm not entirely sure what a professional would say. I hope that's okay? I just don't want to assume I know better than a doctor.
Do you think that anyone, no matter how closely they looked, could possibly not see the droop and unevenness in your face?

I... I know I keep saying the same things, and I really hope I'm not frustrating you by repeating myself. I want to say yes, that maybe someone could look closely and not see it... especially since people do sometimes tell me I look fine. I really try to believe them, I do. I want to be reasonable about this. 

But... it's just so hard because I literally cannot stop seeing this droop and the unevenness around my mouth and jaw. It's there in absolutely every photo, every single time I catch my reflection. Even if someone else says they don't see it, it just feels so terribly obvious to me... to the point where, like I mentioned, it's why I've started avoiding my presentations and hiding from my clients. That's really why I'm here, because I just can't escape it, no matter what anyone else says or how hard I try to ignore it. 

Does that make sense? I just want to make sure I'm answering your question the right way. I really don't want to sound completely irrational.
Do you think that the droop and unevenness in your face are something that only you can see?

Oh, dear... I feel like I'm just talking in circles, and I am so sorry if I'm making your job difficult today. I would absolutely love to say yes, that it's entirely just me. And... well, since people do tell me I look fine, maybe it really is just something in my own head. I try so hard to hold onto that and be rational about it. 

But... oh, it's just so embarrassing to admit... even if I am the only one who sees it, I just can't stop seeing it. The unevenness and the droop around my mouth and jaw, it's just glaring at me in every single photo and every time I pass a mirror. It just feels so completely obvious to me, which is... well, it's exactly why I'm here. Because it feels so real to me that it's making me avoid my work presentations and hide from my clients. 

I know I keep bringing that up, and I know how foolish it sounds for a woman my age to be so caught up in this... I just don't know how to turn it off, even when people say I look fine. Did I answer that okay? I really want to be helpful and give you the right information.
Do you think that the droop and unevenness in your face could be something that isn't actually there, but rather a product of your own perception?

I... I really want to say yes. I would love nothing more than for you to tell me that it's all just in my head and that I'm completely imagining it. It would be such a relief, honestly. And I know I've said this already, and I'm so sorry to keep repeating myself, but I do try to tell myself that when my husband or my friends say I look fine, they're right and I'm wrong. I really do want to be a sensible person about this.

But... oh, it's just so hard. Because even if it is just my perception, it doesn't *feel* like it's just my perception. The droop... the unevenness around my jawline and mouth... it's just there. Every time I look in the mirror, every time I see a photograph, it's all I can focus on. It feels so glaringly obvious to me. 

And that's... well, that's the whole reason I came to see you. Because even if it's just me seeing it, it's ruined my confidence. It's why I'm backing out of my architecture presentations and finding excuses not to meet with my clients face-to-face. I'm just so ashamed of how I look. 

I know that probably sounds terrible, and I hope you don't think I'm completely out of touch with reality. I'm really trying my best to answer you properly... does that make sense? I just don't want to give you the wrong impression.
Do you think that if you were shown a photo of yourself where the droop and unevenness were digitally removed, you would still see them?

Oh... um... that's a really interesting question. I... I hope I'm understanding what you're asking. If someone fixed a photo so the droop and the unevenness were gone... would I still see it? 

I... I want to say no. I really want to say that if it was fixed, I'd finally be able to see myself normally. That would be wonderful, wouldn't it? And I do try so hard to be rational when people tell me I look fine as I am right now. I really do.

But... oh, I'm so sorry, I feel like I'm just giving you the exact same answer again, and I really don't want to be frustrating you. It's just... I'm here because I literally cannot stop seeing this droop around my mouth and my jaw. It's all I see in every single photo and every reflection. So... if someone showed me a fixed photo, I... I'm afraid I might still look for it. Because even when people say it's not there now, it just feels so terribly obvious to me. It's so obvious that it's why I'm hiding from my clients and avoiding my architecture presentations. 

I know that makes me sound completely ridiculous, a woman my age acting like this. I'm so sorry. Did I answer your question okay? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information.
Do you think that your face actually looks the way you describe it, regardless of what others see?

I... I really want to say no. I want to agree with everyone else. I know I'm probably starting to sound like a broken record, and I'm so sorry for taking up so much of your time with this. I really do want to be a cooperative patient, and I want to believe my husband and my friends when they say I look perfectly fine. 

But... oh, it's just so embarrassing to admit this out loud... to me, it really does look exactly the way I describe it. I know you must think I'm incredibly vain or foolish, but I just can't stop seeing it. The droop... the unevenness around my mouth and my jaw... it's just right there, staring back at me in every single mirror and every photo. 

Even when people assure me it's not there, it just feels so terribly, undeniably obvious to me. It's so obvious that... well, like I mentioned before, it's why I've been avoiding my clients and finding excuses not to do my architecture presentations. I just can't bear the thought of them looking at my face. 

I'm so sorry, I know that's not the answer you probably want to hear, and I really hope I'm not making your job difficult today. Does that make sense? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information so you can help me.
Do you think your face looks the way you describe it even if no one else can see the droop and unevenness?

I... yes, I suppose I do. I mean, I know we just talked about this, and I'm really trying not to be difficult... I hope you don't think I'm just being stubborn. I know my husband and my friends say they don't see it, and I really, truly want to believe them. I try so hard to just accept their word for it. 

But... well, yes. To me, it still looks exactly like that, even if they can't see it. I just can't stop seeing it. The droop... the way my jaw and mouth look so uneven... it's just always there when I look in the mirror or see a picture. It feels so glaring to me, so obvious, that I just... I can't face people. It's why I've been hiding from my clients and backing out of my presentations at work. 

I know it sounds awful, and I'm so embarrassed to keep admitting it to you. I really want to be sensible about this. Am I making sense? I just want to make sure I'm answering you properly, I don't want to be a bother.
Do you think your face would still look uneven and droopy to you even if a doctor or plastic surgeon examined it and found no abnormalities?

Oh, goodness... I feel terrible because I know I'm basically giving you the exact same answer again, and I really, really don't want to be frustrating you. I know a plastic surgeon is an expert, and I would love to just accept their professional opinion. I really would. I'd want to be a good patient and just listen to them. 

But... um... honestly? Even if a doctor examined me and said there was absolutely nothing wrong... I think I would still see it. I'm so sorry, I know how completely irrational that sounds for a woman my age. It's just... I'm here today because I literally cannot stop seeing this droop and the unevenness around my mouth and my jaw. It's in every single photo, every reflection... it never goes away for me. 

Even when people—and I suppose even if a professional—tell me I look fine, it just feels so overwhelmingly obvious to me. It's so glaring that... well, like I've been saying, it's the whole reason I've been avoiding my clients and skipping my architecture presentations. I just can't bear the thought of them staring at it. 

I hope I'm not making your job too difficult by being so stuck on this. I'm really trying to give you the honest truth so you can help me. Did I answer that okay for you?
Do you think your perception of the droop and unevenness in your face could be considered a delusion?

A delusion? Oh, my... um... I really don't know. That word sounds so... so serious, and I promise I'm not trying to be completely out of touch with reality or anything like that. I really, really don't want you to think I'm... well, crazy. 

I honestly don't know if it's a delusion. Because to me, I see it right there in the mirror, so clearly, every single day. But if you and my husband and everyone else are telling me it's not real... I just don't know what to think anymore. I don't know what to call it. 

I'm so sorry, I feel like I'm not giving you a very helpful answer right now, and I really want to be doing this right. Is it okay that I'm just... not sure? I hope I'm not disappointing you.
Do you think you would still believe the droop and unevenness are there even if everyone around you, including doctors and experts, told you it's not?

Oh... I... I feel terrible because I feel like I'm just repeating myself, and I really don't want to test your patience. You've been so kind to listen to me. 

I suppose... yes. I think I would still believe it's there. Even if everyone in the world told me it wasn't. I know how awful and stubborn that sounds, and I'm so embarrassed to admit it. I really wish I could just flip a switch and see what you all see. I want to believe you, I truly do. 

But when I look in the mirror, it's just... it's right there. The unevenness, the droop... it's all I can see. I'm so sorry, I know that's not what you want to hear, and I don't want to be a difficult patient. I hope you can understand... am I making any sense at all? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information so you can help me.
Do you think it's possible that your concern about the droop and unevenness in your face is something that's mostly in your mind?

Oh... um... I really want to say yes. I truly do. Because you're the doctor, and I know you understand these things so much better than I do. I really want to be a good patient and just agree with you, because I'm sure you're right. 

I try so hard to tell myself it's just my mind playing tricks on me. My husband says that all the time, and I want to believe it so badly. But... oh, I'm so sorry, I feel like I'm just being so difficult again... when I actually look in the mirror, it just doesn't feel like it's only in my head. It looks so physically real to me. 

Maybe... maybe the way I worry about it so much is the part that's in my mind? Like, maybe I'm blowing the unevenness out of proportion? I really don't know for sure. I'm trying my best to look at this rationally, I promise. I just... I don't want to give you the wrong impression. Is... is that an okay answer? I hope I'm making at least a little bit of sense.
Do you think anything could ever convince you that the droop and unevenness in your face are not actually there?

Oh... I... I really wish I could say yes. I'd love to just agree and tell you that there's some kind of test or expert that could finally convince me it's not real. I really want to be that reasonable for you. 

But... it's just so hard when I can't stop seeing it. The droop and the unevenness, specifically right down here around my mouth and my jaw. It's just staring back at me in every single reflection, every photo... even when people tell me I look completely fine. I know I should just take their word for it, and I always smile and thank them because I don't want to be a bother or seem ungrateful, but inside... it just feels so glaringly obvious to me.

I'm actually a little embarrassed to tell you this, because I know I should be more put-together, but... it's gotten to the point where I've started avoiding my work presentations. And even meeting face-to-face with my clients. I'm an architect, so I have to present my designs, but I just can't bear the thought of them staring at my mouth and judging how uneven it is. 

I know that probably sounds so silly and unprofessional... I'm really sorry, I hope you don't think less of me for letting it affect my job like that. I just want to be completely honest with you so you can help me. Does that make sense? I'm really trying my best to explain it right.
Do you think it's possible that your belief in the droop and unevenness is a false belief that is not based in reality?

Oh... a false belief. Um... I... I really want to say yes, just to show you that I'm listening and that I respect your expertise. Because I do, I truly do. You've been so incredibly patient with me. 

But... oh, I feel so terrible, I just don't know if I can honestly say that. I don't know how to look in the mirror, see the droop right there, and tell myself it's completely made up. It just feels so incredibly real to me, even though I know you're trying to help me see it differently. 

I'm so sorry, I know that's probably the exact opposite of what I'm supposed to say, and I hate being difficult. I'm trying so hard to be open-minded about this, I promise. Is it okay that I'm just... not sure? I really hope I'm not frustrating you by not having the right answer.
Do you think your belief in the droop and unevenness is something that you would still hold even if all evidence and expert opinions contradicted it?

Oh... um... I... I guess I'm just not completely sure how to answer that. I really wish I could just say yes or no and give you exactly what you're looking for. I hate to be so indecisive. 

I mean, if every single expert in the world sat me down and showed me proof that it wasn't there... I'd like to think I would believe them. I really would. Because I know I'm not a doctor, and I don't want to seem like I'm ignoring science or being stubborn. I always try to listen to the professionals. 

But... oh, I'm so sorry, I just... I don't know if I could ever fully turn off that voice in my head, or unsee what I see in the mirror. I'd probably just think that maybe the tests missed something, or... or that I'm just the one weird case they can't figure out. 

Does that make me sound completely unreasonable? I'm so sorry if it does. I really am trying to be rational about all of this. I just... I don't know for sure what I would do. I hope that's an acceptable answer... I'm really trying my best here.
Do you think your belief in the droop and unevenness would change if you received treatment and your perception of it didn't?

Oh... um... that's a really good question. I... I want to say yes, of course. I really want to believe that whatever treatment you suggest will fix everything, because I trust you completely. You're the expert, and I know you're just trying to help me get better. 

But... if I still saw it in the mirror, exactly the same way I do now? Oh, I don't know... I feel like I'd just be right back where I started. I mean, I'd probably pretend it was better, just so I wouldn't disappoint you after you put so much effort into helping me. I'd hate to be a burden or make you feel like your treatment didn't work. 

But deep down... if I still look uneven to myself, I just don't see how I could ever really believe it's gone. I'm so sorry, I know that sounds terrible and uncooperative. I really don't mean to be. I just... I want to be honest so you know what you're dealing with. Is that... is it okay that I feel that way? I hope I'm not making things too difficult for you.
